newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Kohl congratulates Blair, thanks "Dear John".
newsitem.headline: Kohl congratulates Blair, thanks "Dear John".

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Friday congratulated new British Prime Minister Tony Blair and thanked predecessor John Major for his work in strengthening friendly relations between their two countries.

"The continuation and deepening of cooperation based on trust has special significance given the huge future tasks in Europe," Kohl wrote in a telegram to Blair sent from Australia, his latest destination on a Pacific Rim tour.
Kohl arrived in Australia's tropical north on Friday after visiting the sultanate of Brunei.
Kohl said European and Western allies could only conquer the challenges they face on the verge of the next century "together and shoulder to shoulder".
The basic course for addressing these challenges would be set in the weeks ahead, he said.
In a telegram addressed "Dear John", Kohl thanked the departing Prime Minister for cooperation on behalf of Germany.
"It is my particular wish...to thank you for good personal and above all friendly cooperation, which has meant much to me," Kohl wrote to Major.

Earlier, Kohl said he hoped Blair would support the European Union more than the Conservative government had. Offering his cooperation with the new prime minister, Kohl said he would meet Blair the week after next and expected to get to know him better at an EU summit later this month.
"This is an overwhelming mandate for the new government," said Kohl, whose strongly pro-European policies irritated Conservative "Eurosceptics".
One Conservative campaign poster portrayed him as a pro-EU ventriloquist with Blair as a dummy on his knee.

"Voters did not like the anti-European rhetoric of the past few days and weeks and this should be a lesson for all those who want to win votes with anti-European polemics," Kohl told reporters travelling with him in Brunei.
Asked about Blair's stand on the EU's planned economic and monetary union (EMU), Kohl said he had read the Labour policy platform carefully and found it cautious on this point.
"I would welcome it if Labour were more friendly towards Europe than the Conservatives were," he said.
The chancellor announced last month he would run for a record fifth term next year, mostly because he wanted to stay on to see Europe's single currency launched in 1999.

One potential Social Democrat challenger, Gerhard Schroeder, has been toying with a mildly anti-European campaign to exploit German voters' distaste at the idea of giving up the strong mark for the euro currency.
